paper_metadata.title: Question-Answer Extraction from Scientific Articles Using Knowledge Graphs and Large Language Models
paper_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the 48th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR ’25)
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper extracts key concepts and contributions from scientific articles as question-answer pairs. It proposes a Core Context-based QA Generation approach that selects salient paragraphs, uses a large language model to generate and rank questions, and generates answers. Its second approach constructs a knowledge graph by fine-tuning an entity-relationship extraction model on scientific articles, extracts salient triplets using graph and TF-IDF-like saliency measures, and uses them to generate questions and answers. Subject Matter Expert evaluations indicate that the KG-based approach captures article main ideas effectively, and fine-tuning the entity-relation extraction model is important for high-quality triplet extraction.

paper_metadata-abstract-05-01.excerpt: We propose two distinct approaches for generating QAs. The first approach involves selecting salient paragraphs... The second approach leverages a Knowledge Graph (KG) for QA generation. We construct a KG by fine-tuning an Entity Relationship (ER) extraction model on scientific articles... Our evaluations demonstrate that the KG-based approach effectively captures the main ideas discussed in the articles.

code_and_data_availability-28-02.section: Fine-tuning LLMs on the QA dataset

problem_addressed: The paper addresses the difficulty researchers face when identifying and understanding the main ideas, contributions, and novelty of large numbers of scientific articles. It aims to generate concise, targeted QA pairs from full-text articles, with the KG-based method additionally representing article content in the context of the broader literature so that questions can focus on salient and potentially novel information.

methodology.description: The paper presents two sequential QA-generation pipelines. CCQG parses XML articles into paragraphs, represents the title, abstract, and keywords as a proxy, selects paragraphs whose sentence-transformer similarity exceeds a threshold, prompts GPT-3.5 to generate questions, ranks and filters questions, generates answers from associated paragraphs, and removes answers flagged by SelfCheckGPT. The KG-based pipeline selects representative seed documents using TopicBert topic clusters and KMeans, prompts an LLM to extract entity-relation triplets from article chunks, fine-tunes domain-specific REBEL models, builds a per-article KG in Neo4j, computes triplet saliency from entity/triplet TF-IDF, PageRank, graph structure, and semantic similarity to metadata, then prompts GPT-3.5 with salient triplets and paragraphs to generate and rank questions and answers.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: No external ontology is reported. The KG uses an entity-relation-triplet schema consisting of head entity, relationship, and tail entity, and stores per-article entity and triplet frequencies in a Neo4j graph database.

evaluation.setting: The study uses automatic GPT-4-as-judge evaluations for triplets and salient triplets, and both SME and automatic evaluations for QA quality. Two SMEs score each QA on a 1–3 scale; automatic evaluations use the same criteria. QA experiments use 20 articles per domain and top-five QAs per article, while triplet experiments use 50 Computer Science articles.

value: In SME question evaluation, KG outperformed CCQG in both domains. Computer Science: relevance 0.93 vs 0.86, specificity 0.94 vs 0.90, clarity 0.91 vs 0.85. Life Sciences: relevance 0.95 vs 0.83, specificity 0.94 vs 0.81, clarity 0.94 vs 0.82.

In SME answer evaluation, KG outperformed CCQG on every listed metric in both domains. Computer Science KG scores were relevance 0.92, factuality 0.92, specificity 0.87, completeness 0.89, grammatical correctness 0.99, and reference relevance 0.90. Life Sciences KG scores were 0.95, 0.95, 0.92, 0.92, 0.92, and 0.94 respectively.

Automatic QA evaluation showed smaller differences. In Life Sciences, KG scored 0.80/0.80/0.92/0.88/0.99/0.84 for question relevance, answer relevance, question specificity, answer completeness, grammatical correctness, and reference relevance as tabulated; the paper reports automatic evaluation as a lower-bound assessment.
Fine-tuned REBEL achieved a 73.5% cross-model win rate and 0.78 model-specific accuracy, compared with 26.5% and 0.58 for vanilla REBEL.
The full graph-plus-semantic saliency method achieved the highest salient-triplet performance in the reported Figure 6 comparison; triplet IDF outperformed frequency-only ranking.
The GPT-3.5 whole-article baseline had the lowest average QA quality in Figure 5, supporting the importance of content selection.
For downstream fine-tuning, zephyr-7b-beta achieved ROUGE-1/2/L/LSUM of 0.89/0.75/0.86/0.86 for question generation and 0.96/0.93/0.96/0.96 for answer generation.

evidence.excerpt: The results indicate that the KG-based approach achieves a better SME score in terms of all metrics in both domains.

value: The KG-based pipeline incorporates corpus-level context and graph structure, allowing triplet saliency to reflect both article-specific importance and prevalence across the literature.

In the reported SME evaluation, the KG method consistently produced more relevant, specific, and clear questions and more relevant, factual, complete, grammatical, and reference-connected answers than CCQG in both domains.
Fine-tuning REBEL on representative scientific-domain data substantially improved triplet quality over the off-the-shelf model.

value: Review-level inference: the paper's principal output is QA pairs rather than a complete, validated knowledge graph; graph construction serves as an intermediate representation for QA generation.
The evaluation is concentrated on Computer Science and Life Sciences corpora from one publisher, limiting demonstrated domain and source diversity.
The automatic QA evaluation is explicitly described as a lower-bound assessment and does not distinguish the methods as clearly as SME evaluation.

Review-level inference: LLM-generated ER supervision and GPT-based judging introduce dependence on model-generated labels and evaluators, while the paper does not report a conventional human gold-standard triplet benchmark.

The paper leaves unresolved whether corpus-level triplet saliency remains reliable when the reference corpus is smaller, less representative, or from a different source.
The paper leaves unresolved how to scale human evaluation beyond the reported 200 QA sample while maintaining reliable expert judgments.
